say: You give it a formula that claims to give the sum, or the $n$th term, of a pattern. It proves the formula is true for **every** $n$, not just the ones you tried.
The key idea is induction: show it works for $n = 1$, then show that if it works for one number $k$, it must work for the next one, $k+1$. Each case then pulls the next one along.

how.higher: Higher level asks for it as the last part of a long Paper 1 question (2020 and 2025), usually as a proof by induction worth 15 marks.

example.question: Prove by induction that $2 + 4 + 6 + \dots + 2n = n(n+1)$ for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

steps.title: Check n equals 1
steps.say: Test the formula on the first case, $n = 1$. The sum has one term, so check both sides give the same number.

lines.text: Both sides are $2$. So $P(1)$ is true.

steps.title: Assume it works for k
steps.say: Now assume the formula is true for $n = k$. This is the statement $P(k)$ and you may use it.

steps.title: Prove it for k plus 1
steps.say: Now look at $n = k+1$. Add the next term, $2(k+1)$, to both sides of $P(k)$. The left side becomes the sum up to $k+1$. Replace the old sum with $\hl{1}{k(k+1)}$.

lines.text: This is the formula with $n = k+1$: $(k+1)\big((k+1)+1\big)$.

steps.title: Write the conclusion
steps.say: Say what you have shown. A proof by induction is not finished without this sentence.

lines.text: $P(1)$ is true. If $P(k)$ is true then $P(k+1)$ is true. So $P(n)$ is true for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

higher.tip: End with the full conclusion. Leaving out part or all of it costs a mark, even if the algebra is perfect.

The base case and the assumption $P(k)$ can come in either order. Both must be written down.

sources.quote: Steps 1 and 2 can be in any order.

higher.tip: Close the proof with a sentence saying it is true for $n = k+1$ if true for $n = k$, and true for $n = 1$.

say: You give it a geometric series with first term $a$ and common ratio $r$, where $r$ is between $-1$ and $1$. It gives back the **sum** of all the terms, even though there are infinitely many.
The key idea: when $|r| < 1$ the terms shrink towards zero, so the total settles at a fixed number, $S_\infty = \dfrac{a}{1-r}$.

how.higher: Higher level uses it almost every year on Paper 1, either as a part of its own worth 5 or 10 marks or as the last step in a longer question about a dose, a pattern of shapes or a value of $x$.

example.question: Find the sum to infinity of the series $20 + 12 + 7{\cdot}2 + \dots$

steps.title: Find a and r
steps.say: The first term is $\hl{1}{a}$. The common ratio $\hl{2}{r}$ is any term divided by the one before it.

steps.title: Check r is allowed
steps.say: The sum to infinity only exists when $|r| < 1$. Check it before you use the formula.

lines.text: $|\hl{2}{r}| = \frac{3}{5} < 1$, so the series has a sum to infinity.

higher.tip: Check $|r| < 1$ and say so. If $|r| > 1$ there is no sum to infinity, and the marks drop to low partial credit at most.
Write the formula $S_\infty = \dfrac{a}{1-r}$ and substitute into it. Partial credit is given for the formula with some substitution.
If $x$ is unknown, test each value you find. Substitute it, work out $r$, and reject the one that gives no sum to infinity.

say: You give it a geometric series and a target, such as a term that must pass a value. It finds the **number of terms** $n$ needed.
The key idea: $n$ sits in a power, so take logs to bring it down. Then round $n$ to a whole number the right way.

how.higher: Higher level asks for it on Paper 1 (and once on Paper 2, in 2015), as a 10 or 15 mark part: on which day or swing does a value first pass or drop below a target.
how.ordinary: Ordinary level asked it once, in 2023, as a 5 mark part about cases doubling every 5 days.

example.question: A geometric sequence has first term $3$ and common ratio $2$. Find the least value of $n$ for which $T_n > 5000$.

steps.title: Write the nth term
steps.say: Write $T_n = ar^{n-1}$ with $a = 3$ and $r = 2$. Then set it greater than $5000$.

steps.title: Isolate the power
steps.say: Divide both sides by $3$, so the power stands on its own.

steps.title: Take logs
steps.say: Take $\ln$ of both sides. The power $\hl{1}{n-1}$ comes down in front. $\ln 2$ is positive, so the inequality keeps its direction when you divide by it.

steps.title: Round up to a whole number
steps.say: $n$ counts terms, so it is a whole number. It must be bigger than $11{\cdot}70$, so the least value is $12$.

higher.tip: If you solve by trial and improvement, you must evaluate the term just before and just after the crossing point to get full marks.

higher.tip: Take logs of both sides and bring the index down. A log equation without indices earns high partial credit.
When you divide by a log of a ratio smaller than $1$ the number is negative, so the inequality turns around. Say why you flip it.

ordinary.tip: Keep doubling, step by step, until you pass the target. Repeated doubling earns marks even without a formula.
Write each day with its value in a list, and stop at the first day over the target.

say: You give it a recurring decimal such as $0.272727\dots$ It gives back the same number as a **fraction**.
The key idea: a recurring decimal is a geometric series. The repeating block is the first term $a$, and shifting along one block multiplies by $r = \frac{1}{10^k}$, so $S_\infty$ gives the fraction.

example.question: Write $0.272727\dots$ as a fraction in its simplest form, using the sum to infinity.

steps.title: Split into a series
steps.say: Write the decimal as a sum of the repeating blocks.

lines.text: Each block is $\frac{1}{100}$ of the one before. It is a geometric series.

steps.title: Find a and r
steps.say: The first block is $\hl{1}{a}$. Each term is $\frac{1}{100}$ times the last, so $\hl{2}{r} = 0.01$.

steps.title: Use the formula
steps.say: $|r| < 1$, so the series has a sum to infinity. Put $\hl{1}{a}$ and $\hl{2}{r}$ into $S_\infty = \dfrac{a}{1-r}$.
